Hi guys,

I played in the tournament Amsterdam yesterday, and i was thinking
about some things,...

The first, i was 6th on basis of those "stayingpoints" (can't remember
the real name ...)
I haven't read it yet, but how does that work, how many points does
who get? (And does that mean that if your prey sweeps the table you
get the most points apart from your prey? If that is the case i think
it should change, your prey sweeped, because you let him...)

And second, coming for that...i only won 1 (4-player-) table, and got
1 vicpoint somewhere else, and that ALMOST got me in THE FINALS...
Sure, i wouldn't have mind playing the finals, but it sounds strange
to me that playing 1 good game can get you to the finals....
I haven't given it much thought, but wouldn't it be better if decks
that get victory-points in ALL games got to the finals (and at least 1

There's been a very long thread on the merits and flaws of the Game Wins
system. My main argument for the Game Wins system ( which is similar to a
lot of other's ) is that the objective of the game is to win. The Game Wins
system makes the objective of the rounds the same as the finals ( to win
individual games ). If you have a deck that gains 2 VPs every game but
doesn't ( and usually wont ) win games with those 2 VPs then it's no good.
Sure, it's consistent, but it's consistent in loosing, not winning. Give me
a 1 in 3 sweep the table deck any day.

If sometimes you get 2 VPs and occasionally 3VPs then you have a good deck
and you'll most likely get into the finals. But if you can't get that 3rd VP
often enough, you need to change it or play it differently.

The rounds + final system could be considered inherently flawed, but as long
as we have that system, the Game Wins system for ranking is makes much more
sense.

I think you can find an explanation of Tournament Points on the White
Wolf site. Either that, or D-L the Archon.

I have a vague recollection that what you mention is true: the last
player to leave the table has slightly more points than the first, all
other factors being equal.

It is indeed a good question whether you should 'reward' letting the
prey sweep... on the other hand, you are neither the first person
kicked off the table - also a signal of weakness. And I'm sure that
'letting the prey sweep' is not a valid tactic for 3 rounds in a row
in a tournament ;)

> And second, coming for that...i only won 1 (4-player-) table, and got
> 1 vicpoint somewhere else, and that ALMOST got me in THE FINALS...
> Sure, i wouldn't have mind playing the finals, but it sounds strange
> to me that playing 1 good game can get you to the finals....

Well, it's just a matter of calculation, average performance, and
chance. With a total of 22 players (as in Amsterdam), and 5 tables,
there are 81 VP's available over the whole of 3 rounds. That's 3.7 VP
a person 'on average', but there will be games that time out, scoring
a whole lot less points.

So, with some people scoring heavily, and some poorly, you will
certainly be ahead of the pack (I count 6 vp for you, but I do not
know whether you had a 'sweep'). Then again, you ALSO have a
Table/Game win, which is rated as more important than just getting
VPs.

And anyway, you wouldn't want to play the final, but go to eat in that
student cafe, since the food was good. ;)

> I haven't given it much thought, but wouldn't it be better if decks
> that get victory-points in ALL games got to the finals (and at least 1
> tablewin) ? I mean, those decks are obviously least screwed by table
> position, and show the most stable performance...

Well, there's always the deck that has been discussed earlier - the
weenie computer hack deck. It can probably always take 1 VP at each
table, no more. It cannot sweep a table and will in all likelyhood
never win the final. And, in the final, the winner is the person able
to kill and keep alive the most - the person who most closely
approaches the Table Sweep. So it is 'good' to reward peak performance
in a few places over adequate mean performance.

(If the tournament rules said that the final winner is the person that
had most VPs in all 4 rounds summed, your argument would hold out
better).

> What do you think?

That next time I want to sit at a table with you and Tim and Pepijn
and Mike.

Tobias
Deventer

No. Ousting order (timing) is not tracked. Tournament Points are

12 TP. Tied positions split TPs.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Wouter Kuyper" <wouter...@yahoo.com> wrote in message
news:155a2de5.02050...@posting.google.com...



Interesting idea. If I understand you right, you'd use this
scoring to determine who gets into the finals:

1. Games Won
2. VPs earned in games not won
3. Tournament Points

I'm not sure how much of a difference this would end up making -
it'd probably affect ranking going into the finals (and therefore
who gets to decide where to sit last), but as long as game wins
are still most important, you'll only be able to get into the
finals (generally) with at least one game win, and winning more
than one game would still be better than winning only one.

I guess the practical effect of subtracting out "how much you won
by when you won" would be that the first tiebreaker would become
"how well you did when you lost" rather than "how well you did
when you won and lost put together". Compared to the current
system, it ranks non-sweeping decks higher. (The current system
favors sweeping decks because getting 5 VPs and winning a table
is substantially better than getting 3 VPs to win the table, at
the moment. They'd be equivalent under this proposal.)

I doubt that the end result would be enough of a change to have
any large effect on who gets into final games. It's also pretty
hard to say with any great certainty that particular decks "always
sweep" or "always score"; it'd probably have fairly random effects
most of the time. At a guess, anyway. :-)

Josh

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Wouter Kuyper" <wouter...@yahoo.com> wrote in message
news:155a2de5.02050...@posting.google.com...

> True, but i am arguing that it might be broke, if it takes only 1 good

> game to get to the finals...then you only need 1 weak predator...

Ah, I see. I don't know if this can "fix" that, though. If
a tournament is small enough that you can make it to the finals
with only one game win (in my experience, any tournament with
25 players or less will probably have at least some finalists
with only one GW), then it would still take only one "good"
game to make the finals. I suppose the effect would be that,
if one player had 5 VPs and 1 GW from one round and 0 VPs/GWs
in the other two, and a second player had 3 VPs and 1 GW from
one round and 2 VPs/0 GWs from the other two, the second player
would be ranked higher (instead of tied-except-for-TPs) than
the first. But is it really better to "win by a narrower margin"
in one game and "lose by a narrower margin" in another than to
"win by a lot" and "lose by a lot"? A matter of taste, I think.
And if you end up having any people that actually *do* have game
wins where they only had 3 VP (or less), that seems to contradict
your intuition that "if you get a couple VPs, it's easy to get
the rest".

> I think this approach minimizes the luck of seating order, because you
> need to be able to "play" at at least two different tables

True if not all the 1-GW players make the finals (and yeah, in
most tournaments with at least 15 players I think not *all* the
players with 1 GW generally make the finals). But there might
not be enough of them who got VPs in games they didn't win for
this tiebreaker to make much difference, either.

Example: In the last local tournament, there were 15 players.
After three rounds, five had one GW and one had two GWs (two
GWs were "lost" by tables that timed out). Of the 1-GW players,
"total VPs" were 5.5, 4.5, 4, 4, 3. "VPs in games not won"
were 0.5, 0.5, 0, 0, 0. So in this example, the first and
second player under the current system would still have been
first and second; the next tiebreaker either would replicate
the existing system ("total VPs") or potentially slightly
alter it. (if TPs was the only other tiebreaker - for these
players, TPs were 120, 120, 108, 102, 108, so the 3-VPs
player would have taken the place of the second 4-VPs player
if TPs were the only tiebreaker after "VPs in games not won".)

I think what this points to is that it's hard to get VPs at
all, let alone get them in more than one game. :-) So I'd
guess that not too many one-game-win players are ever going
to have very many "VPs in games not won" to use for this
tiebreaker. Even more so for two-game-win players - they
only played in one game that they didn't win.

Basically I get the idea you want to make it "harder" to
win tournaments - less luck-based... which I'd say is a
worthy goal, but given the same players under any system,
and no way of reducing the effects of luck within any
single game, we probably don't have - without playing more
preliminary rounds - any really good way to better determine
who's done better on the day than "Game Wins, then total
VPs, then Tournament Points".

For whatever that's worth...

Josh
